posts.title: Looped Language Models Improve Compositional Tool Calling

comments.content:
The adaptive inference approach seems critical here but I wonder how well it actually works when you're dealing with unpredictable real world API failures or rate limits. If the model allocates more computation loops to a problem that ultimately hits a timeout or quota error, you've just burned extra tokens and latency for nothing. The benchmarks mentioned are synthetic and assume APIs behave deterministically, but in production you're constantly dealing with transient errors, schema drift, and authentication edge cases that break the compositional chain halfway through.

I'd be curious to see how the looped approach handles recovery and backtracking when a middle step in a multi API workflow fails. Does it retry with adjusted parameters? Does it cache intermediate state so you don't recompute everything from scratch? The paper focuses on accuracy improvements but the practical deployment question is whether the added complexity of managing recurrent depth and adaptive stopping criteria is worth it compared to just building explicit retry logic and state machines around a standard LLM. For simple two or three step compositions maybe the engineering overhead isn't justified, but for genuinely complex workflows with branching dependencies this could be valuable if the infrastructure supports it cleanly.

comments.content:
On one level this looks like straightforward price discrimination. SSO is a reliable enterprise signal, so vendors put it behind a paywall that maps to procurement checklists. It also carries real support costs. SAML in particular is a swamp of brittle metadata and edge cases, and being on-call for every IdP nuance is not a hobby. The paywall is less about greed than about finding a metered surface that enterprises expect to fund.

But zoom out and the choice of where to put the tollbooth shapes the ecosystem. Identity is drifting toward utility status, like TLS did a decade ago. When SSO is gated, smaller teams either accept weaker auth, roll their own, or consolidate further under the big platforms that bundle identity for free because they monetize elsewhere. That nudges the market toward centralization. The economics make sense for vendors, yet the externality is a slower march toward security by default.

There is also a category error lurking here. In a self-hosted world, authentication is the boundary, not a feature. Charging for SCIM, group-based policy, advanced role mapping, audit exports, incident response playbooks, and white-glove support feels aligned with enterprise value. Charging to plug the app into the identity a company already runs feels like taxing the doorknob. Open core depends on community adoption, and this specific gate sits exactly where adoption begins.

Perhaps the path forward is to treat baseline OIDC SSO as table stakes and monetize assurance and operations instead. Make the safe path the default, then charge for scale, compliance, and care. Projects that do this tend to see wider grassroots uptake and, paradoxically, more enterprise deals, because procurement follows where the users already went.

This is just another manifestation of the same pattern we see across the entire tech landscape functionality being carved out and monetized as "enterprise features." SSO has become the new PDF export - a basic expectation that gets locked behind arbitrary pricing tiers to extract maximum revenue from organizations that have no choice but to pay.

The irony is that these self-hosted projects often started as reactions against proprietary vendor lock-in, yet they're recreating the exact same extraction mechanisms. A company with 50 employees suddenly needs to justify $10k annually just so their developers don't have to manage yet another set of credentials. It's the SaaS playbook applied to open source, then hold essential operational requirements hostage.

What's particularly cynical is how authentication - arguably the most security-critical component - becomes a luxury feature. We're teaching an entire generation of developers that proper identity management is optional unless you can afford the premium tier. posts.title: Run GLM-OCR, DeepSeek-OCR-2, Dots.mocr with an OpenAI Compatible API
posts.text:
Open-weight OCR VLMs have advanced significantly over the past year, yet most teams still rely on frontier VLMs for document parsing because researching, evaluating, and deploying the right models remains challenging.

So we built VLM Run Gateway: one OpenAI-compatible endpoint for open-weight OCR and VLM models. One-line change to switch models, and parse 100K+ pages for under $60.

Model Catalog: PP-OCRv6 (22M), GLM-OCR (0.9B), dots.mocr (3B), DeepSeek-OCR-2 (3B), PaddleOCR-VL (0.9B), and Florence-2-large (770M). Different models win on different document classes — dense legal text, scanned healthcare forms, construction drawings — which is the reason the catalog exists rather than a single default.

Try the Colab Quickstart: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1RkuVIyuc5Po-UlcSlFyJCam5tjCm9IHM?usp=sharing

Document orchestration built in: Send a PDF URL and we rasterize it, distribute pages across workers, preserve page order, stream completed pages, retry failures, and isolate OOMs. Switch to a new model, and you get the same pipeline orchestration and the new model's performance.

OpenAI-compatible API + MCP: For API integrations into your workflows, use JSON mode with a strongly typed output contract. For agents, we ship an MCP server at `https://gateway.vlm.run/mcp` with a `read_document` tool that provides the same cost-efficient parsing, especially for long-form documents. Any MCP-compatible client (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and others) can now consume visual content natively and cost-efficiently.

Cost-efficient: Frontier VLMs are still the right choice for open-ended reasoning, where the task is “figure out what this means” rather than “parse this.” But for extraction, OCR, layout, and parsing, they’re an expensive default. At production scale, the cost difference is significant, often 10x. Every Gateway response includes `usage.cost`, so you can run the same documents through multiple models and compare the exact costs yourself.

Try it out quickly via our CLI:

$ pip install vlmrun

$ vlmrun config set --api-key 'vlmrun' # anon-user, rate-limited

$ vlmrun gw models

$ vlmrun gw chat <doc>.pdf -m zai-org/glm-ocr

$ vlmrun gw chat <doc>.pdf -m zai-org/glm-ocr --json-mode

$ vlmrun gw chat <doc>.pdf -m deepseek-ai/deepseek-ocr-2

$ vlmrun gw chat <doc>.pdf -m rednote-hilab/dots.mocr

$ vlmrun gw chat <doc>.pdf -m paddleocr/pp-ocrv6

[1] Docs: https://docs.vlm.run/gateway

[2] Catalog: https://docs.vlm.run/gateway/models

[3] MCP: https://docs.vlm.run/gateway/mcp-server

Run multiple documents across models in our catalog and tell us which performs best. We’re especially interested in workloads where the results are surprising.

comments.content: This accessibility breakthrough could democratize specialized OCR for smaller teams and indie developers who couldn't justify frontier VLM costs before. At scale, that $60 per 100K pages pricing feels transformative—suddenly complex document parsing becomes viable for countless new applications beyond big tech budgets.

OpenAI-compatible routing for open-weight OCR is the obvious waypoint to commoditization. First order, you cut frontier spend by 5 to 10x for structured extraction. comments.content:
There is a structural tension in this space worth naming. We have spent the last two years treating vision models as general reasoning engines, asking them to both perceive and interpret in a single forward pass. That conflation was inevitable when frontier models were the only option with sufficient capability, but it also created a cost structure that doesn't align with the actual task distribution in production systems.

Most document processing pipelines are not asking open-ended questions. They are asking structured extraction questions where the schema is known in advance and the variance is in layout, scanning quality, or language mixing. The economic logic changes dramatically when you can decompose "understand this document" into a perception step that costs pennies and a reasoning step that costs dollars, and only invoke the expensive component when semantic interpretation is genuinely required. This is not just cost optimization. It changes what you can afford to build, which changes the set of viable products.

What makes this shift interesting is that it mirrors an older pattern in computer vision. Before deep learning, OCR was a solved narrow task and scene understanding was intractable. Then for a brief period everything collapsed into end-to-end models. Now we are re-discovering specialization, but at a higher capability baseline. The open weight ecosystem is enabling that re-discovery by making it feasible to run task-specific models at scale without negotiating enterprise contracts or managing complex deployments. The API compatibility layer matters because it lowers the switching cost to near zero, which means teams can actually experiment with this decomposition rather than just talking about it.

This post introduces VLM Run Gateway, a unified service that simplifies using specialized open-source OCR and vision-language models through an OpenAI-compatible API. The core problem it solves is the friction in deploying diverse OCR models—like GLM-OCR or DeepSeek-OCR-2—which excel at specific tasks (e.g., dense text vs. technical drawings) but are cumbersome to test and integrate individually. Instead of forcing teams to manage each model’s infrastructure, this gateway lets you swap models with a single parameter change while handling document processing pipelines automatically.

What makes this practical is the built-in orchestration for real-world documents. You send a PDF URL, and the service rasterizes pages, distributes work across parallel workers, preserves page order, streams results incrementally, and retries failures—all while isolating crashes like out-of-memory errors. For integration, it supports standard OpenAI-style API calls with JSON mode for structured outputs, plus an MCP server compatibility layer that lets AI agents (like Claude or Codex) natively "read" visual content through a `read_document` tool. This bridges a gap for cost-sensitive parsing tasks where frontier VLMs are overkill.

The cost efficiency here is compelling. While giant models like GPT-4V are great for open-ended reasoning, they’re expensive for straightforward extraction—often 10x pricier at scale. Gateway’s catalog includes leaner models (from 22M to 3B params), and every response includes a `usage.cost` field so you can compare expenses directly. Parsing 100,000 pages reportedly costs under $60, making it viable for bulk processing. Try the Colab quickstart or CLI (`pip install vlmrun`) to test models against your own documents—especially if you handle varied formats like healthcare forms or blueprints—and share which model surprises you!

posts.title: Ask HN: I have an obvious solution to the halting problem does anybody care ?
posts.text:
Pf(x,n) : x is a proof of n
Rf(x,n) : x is a proof of ¬n
Prf(x): x is a proof
Ref(x): x is a disproof
DiophantineFormula(n): n is a Diophantine formula
```
h(n) = y iff ∃x[(y=0∧¬DiophantineFormula(n))∨((Pf(x,n)∨Rf(x,n))∧((y=1∧Prf(x))∨(y=0∧Ref(x))))]
```

inspired by [Refutability as recursive as Provability](https://www.academia.edu/116614094/Refutability_as_recursive_as_Provability)

comments.content:
What this really buys you is a proof searcher wearing a Diophantine hat. The second you tie h(n) to “exists a proof or a refutation,” you have decidability only if your underlying theory is negation complete for Diophantine truth. By MRDP, halting maps to Diophantine solvability, so you have quietly required a complete, sound, recursively axiomatised theory of arithmetic. Pick a concrete exampleine statement. It is true but unprovable in PA; if your Pf/Rf are for PA, h(n) just spins. If you strengthen the system to catch that case, incompleteness pops up elsewhere. You are not deciding halting, you are deciding provability in whichever theory you smuggle in.

Second order effects are predictable. Threads like this multiply as LLMs make syntactic dressings easier, so we get a flood of “obvious” solutions, arXiv mods harden, and search quality on foundational topics degrades. The upside is defensive infrastructure, more problems packaged with machine checkable certificates and more attention to conditional results, for example, halting deciders relative to large cardinal oracles. The downside is that newcomers learn the wrong lesson, which is to rearrange quantifiers until the undecidable looks tame, rather than the right one, which is to choose a theory, state the oracle, and price

comments.content:
This reminds me of a situation a few years back at a startup I was with. We were playing around with some early versions of code generation, not quite LLM-as-policy in the current sense, but more like very sophisticated templating and rule-based systems. The idea was to generate boilerplate and even some simple business logic, which would then be validated. It felt very much like the "world model" approach, where we'd try to synthesize code and then check if it actually did what we wanted.

The problem we kept hitting wasn't so much the generation itself, but the verification step. We had a pretty robust suite of unit and integration tests, but there was always this underlying doubt. Even when the generated code passed all the checks, it was hard to shake the feeling that we might be missing an edge case, or that the tests themselves were implicitly biased by the generation logic. It was a chicken-and-egg situation where the "world model" for generation and the "world model" for verification felt too intertwined.

I'm a little skeptical that even with more advanced LLMs, this fundamental issue completely disappears. It seems like the papers touch on "Play-Adequacy vs Prediction-Accuracy" and "The Sampling-Verification Danger Law," which resonates with that feeling. You can predict what the code *should* do, and you can even verify it against a suite of tests, but if those tests themselves don't capture the full complexity or subtle interactions of the "real world" problem, you're still in a risky spot. comments.content:
This feels like a natural evolution of how we'll need to think about agent reliability once they're running multi-step workflows in production. Right now most people treat LLM uncertainty like it's a stateless problem—you get a probability per token, maybe you ensemble a few runs, and you call it a day. But that completely ignores the compounding nature of errors when an agent makes a dozen tool calls or reasoning steps. If step three was slightly off, and step seven built on that shaky foundation, your final answer might look confident but be completely wrong.

The trajectory graph approach makes a lot of sense. You're essentially building a causal model of how uncertainty flows through the execution history, which should let you pinpoint where things went sideways even if the final output looks superficially reasonable. I'd bet this becomes table stakes for any serious agent deployment within two years. The real question is whether you can make the graph construction and propagation cheap enough to run in real time, or if it ends up being a post-hoc analysis tool. Either way, being able to say "this agent run is 73% confident and here's the step where risk spiked" is going to be hugely valuable for debugging and selective human-in-the-loop interventions.

This could introduce cycles or self-referential paths in the execution history, which aren't strictly linear "trajectories."

Does the framework implicitly assume an acyclic graph for its propagation, or is there a mechanism to gracefully handle these sorts of iterative feedback loops? comments.content:
The core claim here is that modeling uncertainty as a graph propagation problem outperforms local methods like token probabilities or per-step confidence. But I don't see any actual numbers in this abstract, and the theoretical justification for why this should work better is pretty hand-wavy.

First, what does "consistently outperforms" mean quantitatively? Are we talking about a 2% improvement in AUROC or something substantial enough to matter in production? The abstract mentions "more accurate uncertainty estimates" and "earlier failure detection" but gives zero numbers, zero baselines, and zero context on effect size. Without that, this could just be overfitting to three benchmarks.

Second, the graph propagation idea sounds intuitive but also sounds expensive and potentially fragile. How sensitive is this method to graph construction choices? What happens when the "temporal and semantic dependency edges" are themselves uncertain or misspecified? If you're building a directed graph from an execution trace, you're adding a whole layer of modeling assumptions that could easily introduce more noise than signal. The paper needs to show ablations on graph structure and demonstrate that the improvements aren't just coming from throwing more compute at the problem.

Finally, I'm skeptical of any UQ method that claims to solve accumulation of long-range dependencies without addressing the fundamental issue, which is that LLMs don't actually have well-calibrated uncertainty estimates to begin with. Propagating garbage through a graph still gives you garbage. Show me calibration plots, show me how this degrades on out-of-distribution tasks, and show me that this isn't just another way to overfit to validation metrics.

posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok in one place.

Here's a quick 2m demo of how we use Proliferate to build Proliferate: \[demo link\]

I started building Proliferate after my team onboarded to OpenAI Codex. Within the first few days, we were doing basically all our work in Codex itself- using computer use instead of websites, having codex manage agents for us, and setting up automations for recurring work. We really never needed to leave the desktop app to get work done.

If my team’s experience is anything close to representative, a Codex-like app (horizontal agent + a beautiful UI) is in fact the main interface every company is going to use to get work done- which is perfectly in line with OpenAI's mission to make Codex the everything app (see: [https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469)).

Yet after spending a few weeks almost entirely inside that interface, I realized I wanted to build my workflows on something that isn’t inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as we began automating more tasks and exploring open-weight models. I wanted to work with agents from all the labs and not feel more and more tethered to OpenAI.

And that's what Proliferate is for! We are the open-source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across agents and model providers, while building toward Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
* Working with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok with their native inference and configuration options, including Bedrock, Azure, and self hosted inference.
* Inter-agent communication and management: a parent agent can spawn and communicate with another supported agent as a subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs).  
* Building workflows- one of the features I'm most excited about. These are re-usable chains of agent sessions and human approval gates, with the harness and model chosen per step and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process. Some examples are attached here: LINK

All of Proliferate is 100% open source under AGPL-3.0. There are still definitely some rough spots, but we’re building fast and I’d really love any feedback!

posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok in one place.

Here's a quick 2m demo of how we use Proliferate to build Proliferate: \[demo link\]

I started building Proliferate after my team onboarded to OpenAI Codex. Within our first few days of using it, we were doing basically all our work in Codex itself- using computer use instead of websites, having codex manage agents for us, and setting up automations for recurring work. We really never needed to leave the desktop app to get work done

All of which is in line with OpenAI's mission to make Codex the everything app (see: [https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469)).

If my team’s experience is anything close to representative, a Codex-like app (horizontal agent + a beautiful UI) is in fact the main interface every company is going to use to get work done.

Yet after spending a few weeks almost entirely inside that interface, I realized I wanted to build my workflows on something that isn’t inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I began automating more tasks and explored open-weight models. I wanted to work with agents from all the labs and not feel more and more tethered to OpenAI.

And that's what Proliferate is for! We are the open-source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across agents and model providers, while building toward Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
* Working with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok with their native inference and configuration options, including Bedrock, Azure, and self hosted inference.
* Inter-agent communication and management: a parent agent can spawn and communicate with another supported agent as a subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs).  
* Building workflows- one of the features I'm most excited about. These are re-usable chains of agent sessions and human approval gates, with the harness and model chosen per step and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process. Some examples are attached here: LINK

All of Proliferate is 100% open source under AGPL-3.0. There are still definitely some rough spots, but we’re building fast and I’d really love any feedback!

comments.content:
This is precisely the kind of tool we need more of – technically impressive, genuinely open-source, and aiming for interoperability. Kudos for tackling the vendor lock-in problem head-on. Yet, the deeper question remains: even when self-hosted and model-agnostic, what does this level of pervasive automation *do* to the nature of work and the individuals performing it?

The promise is liberation from drudgery, delegating routine coding tasks to agents. But the trajectory described – spending weeks entirely inside the AI interface, automating increasingly complex workflows including code review and PR construction – suggests a profound shift in agency. When the agent manages agents, and workflows become opaque chains of automated steps punctuated by "human approval gates," what becomes of genuine understanding and control? Are we building tools that augment developers, or creating systems where developers become glorified workflow auditors, trusting processes they no longer fully comprehend?

Furthermore, while self-hosting mitigates direct data leakage to third-party vendors, it doesn't eliminate the privacy and fairness concerns inherent in the underlying models themselves. These agents, regardless of provider, are trained on vast, often opaque datasets. They embed biases and make probabilistic judgments. Automating critical processes like code review or QA through chains of these models, even locally, risks amplifying and obscuring those biases within internal systems. The veneer of control self-hosting provides might obscure the fundamental lack of transparency and accountability baked into the AI components themselves.

The allure of efficiency is undeniable, and the technical execution here is commendable. But we must persistently ask: efficiency for whom, and at what cost to human judgment, understanding, and the potential for systemic unfairness? Open-source and self-hosting are necessary steps, but insufficient alone to address these deeper structural questions about agency and the very nature of intellectual work in an automated future. Who controls the controllers, even when they're nominally ours?

posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok in one place.

Here's a quick 2m demo of how we use Proliferate to build Proliferate: DEMO

I started building Proliferate after my team onboarded to OpenAI Codex. Within our first few days of using it, we were doing basically all our work in Codex itself- using computer use instead of websites, having codex manage agents for us, and setting up automations for recurring work. We really never needed to leave the desktop app to get work done

All of which is according to plan and in line with OpenAI's mission to make Codex the everything app (see: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469).

If my team’s experience is anything close to representative, a Codex-like app (horizontal agent in a beautiful UI) is in fact the main interface every person is going to use to get work done.

Yet after spending a few weeks almost entirely inside that interface, I realized I wanted to build my workflows on something that isn’t inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I began automating more tasks and adopting open-weight models. I wanted to work with agents from all the labs.

And that's what Proliferate is for\! We are the open-source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across agents and model providers, while building toward Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
* Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok through their native authentication and inference options, including Bedrock, Azure, and self hosted inference.
* Inter-agent communication and management: a parent agent can spawn and communicate with another supported agent as a subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs).  
* Building workflows- one of the features I'm most excited about. These are linear chains of agent sessions and human approval gates, with the harness and model chosen per step and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process. Some examples are attached here: LINK

All of Proliferate is 100% open source under AGPL-3.0. There are still definitely some rough spots, but we’re building fast and I’d love to any feedback!

Proliferate's multi-agent approach looks promising for avoiding that lock-in.  
Isolated worktrees could've saved us weeks of duct-tape solutions.

comments.content:
The core architectural concept here is isolated worktrees for each agent task. Think of a worktree as a self-contained sandbox: a dedicated Git branch *and* a separate working directory on your filesystem. When Proliferate assigns a task to an agent like Codex or Claude Code, it doesn't just spin up a process; it creates this complete, isolated environment. The agent's terminal session, its conversation history with the model, the specific code changes it makes, and crucially, the state of its Git branch all live exclusively within this worktree. This isolation prevents agents trampling over each other's files or Git state when running in parallel.

This matters because concurrent AI agents modifying the same codebase is inherently messy. Without isolation, Agent A modifying `utils.py` while Agent B is also generating changes to `utils.py` would cause immediate file conflicts and Git chaos. The worktree solves this. Each task operates in its own branch (`agent-task-123`), with its own copy of the files. You can see this isolation clearly during review: inspecting Agent A's changes shows *only* the diffs from its specific worktree branch against the main branch, unaffected by Agent B's concurrent work. It's Git's branching model applied rigorously per-task.

comments.content:
The entire premise here, trying to marry "native harnesses" with "isolated worktree workspaces" and then layer "inter-agent communication" on top, sounds like a recipe for constant frustration. You claim each agent runs through its "native harness," which is fine, that's how they expect to operate. But then you also boast about "isolated worktree workspaces" for *every task*. What happens when a "parent agent" delegates to a "subagent" within a workflow? Does that subagent get a *new* isolated worktree for its subtask, or does it somehow inherit and modify the parent's? The documentation is conveniently vague on this crucial point, and it betrays a fundamental misunderstanding of how these systems actually interact under any real pressure.

If the subagent gets a new worktree, then you're introducing a massive overhead of merging changes back into the parent's branch — exactly the kind of manual, error-prone process these systems are supposed to eliminate. Who owns the conflict resolution there? The user? Or another agent, which just punts the problem to an even less reliable actor? If the subagent operates within the *same* worktree, then the "isolated" claim becomes meaningless, exposing agents with potentially conflicting assumptions to the same mutable state. That's a direct path to chaos as soon as anything non-trivial is attempted.

Real-world development isn't just about passing strings of text between discrete, atomic steps. It involves complex, stateful interactions with a shared codebase, version control, and potentially different toolchains invoked by distinct "native harnesses." Trying to abstract this away with a thin veneer of "inter-agent communication" without robust, clear semantics for how shared state is managed across these separate execution environments is a glaring omission. This isn't some minor bug; it's a foundational design flaw that will become painfully obvious the moment anyone tries to use this for anything more complex than a basic script.

This is a problem every framework attempting to orchestrate disparate tools eventually runs into. Promising "native harness" support alongside seamless, isolated, *and* collaborative workflows with such opaque state management is just naive. posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok in one place.

Here's a quick 2m demo of how I use Proliferate to build Proliferate: [demo link]

I started building Proliferate after onboarding to OpenAI Codex. Within my first few days of using it, I began doing virtually all my knowledge work through Codex- delegating administrative tasks, communicating specs directly to GPT models, and dispatching agents to write code.

And Codex has continued adding features that make it easier to do everything within it: computer use replaced most of my website browsing, its PR review feature replaced most of my GitHub browsing, and cloud agents let me run this kind of work 24/7. This is all in line with OpenAI's mission to make Codex the everything app (see: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469).

But after spending weeks primarily inside the Codex interface, I realized I actually wanted to build my workflows on something not inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I began automating recurring work across my team and adopting open-weight models. I wanted to work with agents from all the labs and be able to share and own the platform where this work was getting done.

And that's what Proliferate is for! We are the open-source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across agents and model providers while building toward Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
- Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok through their native authentication and inference options, including Bedrock for Claude Code.
- Inter-agent communication and management: a parent agent can spawn and communicate with another supported agent as a subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs).
- Building workflows - one of the features I'm most excited about - as linear chains of agent steps and human approval gates, with the harness and model chosen per step and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process.

All of Proliferate is open source under AGPL-3.0. Full control-plane self-hosting is available through Docker Compose, but remains beta.

I'd love to hear which coding agents you're actually mixing day to day, and which repeated workflow you'd want to save and rerun first. I'll be in the comments all day!

comments.content: The framing here is “optionality across agents,” but the real issue is who ends up owning the workflows that quietly become your organization’s nervous system. If people funnel all their dev processes into Codex, or into any single vendor’s IDE, they’re not just locking in a model, they’re handing over long-term control of how work is structured and supervised. An AGPL, self-hostable layer that treats labs as interchangeable backends is closer to how this should work. The danger is that, as teams normalize agent-driven automation, they forget that substitutability and reversibility are ethical requirements, not geeky preferences.

Back in the expert systems and “autonomous agents” phase of the 90s, folks worried about roughly the same thing but used much plainer vocabulary. posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok in one place, each running natively with its own authentication, tools, and configuration options.

Here's a quick 2-minute demo of how I use Proliferate to build Proliferate: [demo link]

I started building Proliferate after onboarding to OpenAI Codex. Within my first few days of using it, I began doing virtually all my knowledge work through Codex- delegating administrative tasks, communicating specs directly to GPT models, and dispatching agents to write code.

And Codex has continued adding features that make it easier to do everything within it: computer use replaced most of my website browsing, its PR review feature replaced most of my GitHub browsing, and cloud agents let me run this kind of work 24/7. This is all in line with OpenAI's mission to make Codex the everything app (see: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469).

Yet after spending weeks primarily inside the Codex interface, I realized I actually wanted to build my workflows on something not inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I began automating recurring work across my team and adopting open-weight models. I wanted to work with agents from all the labs and be able to share and own the platform where this work was getting done.

And that's what Proliferate is for! We are the open-source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across agents and model providers while building toward Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
- Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Grok through their native authentication and inference options, including Bedrock for Claude Code.
- Inter-agent communication and management: a parent agent can spawn and communicate with another supported agent as a subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs).
- Building workflows - one of the features I'm most excited about - as linear chains of agent steps and human approval gates, with the harness and model chosen per step and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process.

All of Proliferate is open source under AGPL-3.0. Full control-plane self-hosting is available through Docker Compose, but remains beta.

I'd love to hear which coding agents you're actually mixing day to day, and which repeated workflow you'd want to save and rerun first. I'll be in the comments all day!

comments.content:
This is exactly the kind of technical masturbation that's eating our industry alive. We've gone from engineers who understood systems deeply to people who think sophistication means chaining together more AI agents to do the thinking for them.

Building "workflows" to automate code review and PR construction? That's called learning your tools and developing judgment, not spawning subagents to delegate the intellectual work that makes you competent in the first place.

The fact that someone considers it progress to spend "weeks primarily inside the Codex interface" rather than actually understanding code is a perfect encapsulation of where we're headed. We're creating a generation of developers who can orchestrate AI but can't debug a segfault or reason about system performance.

posts.text:
Hi HN, I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with any coding agent- Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and more- each running natively with their own authentication, tools, and configuration options.

Here's a quick 2-minute demo of how I use Proliferate to build Proliferate: ()

I started building Proliferate after onboarding to OpenAI Codex. Within a few days of onboarding, I found myself doing virtually all my knowledge work through Codex- delegating administrative tasks, communicating specs directly to GPT models, and dispatching agents to write code.

And Codex has continued adding features that make it easier to never leave the app (computer use, PR review, cloud agents). All of this has made Codex a pretty magical interface for doing... well, everything (see "Codex for everything": https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469).

Yet, after spending weeks primarily inside the Codex interface, I realized I wanted to build my workflows on something not inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I began automating recurring work across my team and adopting open source models.

And that's what Proliferate is for! We are the open source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across OpenAI, Anthropic, self-hosted models, and more, while building a fully featured platform to match Codex's breadth.

Today Proliferate supports:
* Every coding agent through its native authentication and inference options- Bedrock for Claude Code, your Ollama setup for Codex, etc.
* Inter-agent communication and management- any agent can spawn and communicate with any other agent or subagent (I personally like to have Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models reviewing PRs)
* Building workflows- one of the features I'm most excited about- linear chains of agent and human nodes, with the harness/model chosen per node and documents passed between them. I use this to automate code review, QA, and my PR construction process.

All of Proliferate is entirely open source and self-hostable; we're also working on cloud features that let you collaborate across a team with any class of models.

Would love any feedback on how you're using IDEs today and what could make Proliferate a no-brainer for you!

1) computer use good enough that I don't need to visit most websites anymore
2) cloud agents for long running tasks
3) pull requests so I don't even need to visit GitHub

All of this makes Codex a magical product that can genuinely be the single horizontal platform you use to do all your knowledge work (see "Codex for everything": https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469).

Yet as new open source models dropped and I spent weeks inside the Codex interface, I realized I wanted to build my workflows on something that isn't inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I began automating more recurring work across my team and budgeting specifically for token spend.

However, I realized close to nobody was taking this part of the application layer head-on. Instead, most of the true Codex-level IDE options I saw were desktop apps from other foundation model labs - Claude Code's desktop app, xAI's Cursor, etc.

So that's what Proliferate is: an open source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across OpenAI, Anthropic, self-hosted models, and more.

Today we allow you to:
- Work with any coding agent while keeping the native authentication and inference each one offers - your existing inference, whether that's Bedrock for Claude Code or your Ollama setup for Codex. Each harness runs natively rather than through a lowest-common-denominator wrapper, and we never middle-man your inference, so you pay whatever you already pay.
- Skip the provisioning: each agent gets an isolated git worktree and a chat you can drop into, so agents work in parallel without stepping on each other or on you.
- Have your different harnesses communicate and work together through subagents. A parent agent can create another agent in the same workspace - any harness - give it a bounded task, inspect or message it, interrupt it, and receive its result. The child has a durable transcript, and you can promote it into a full session if the thread becomes worth keeping. (I personally love having Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models on review.)
- Run workflows, the feature I'm most excited about: linear chains of agent and human nodes. You select the harness/model for each agent node, declare inputs, and pass durable documents between nodes. A run can stop at a human gate, be approved, or redo earlier work with a steering prompt. We use them to automate our own cross-agent work, and there are templates for code review, QA, and observability [TODO: link to docs].

All of Proliferate is entirely open source and self-hostable. We're working on cloud features that let you collaborate across a team with any class of models.

In the limit, we want to let every company use a world-class agent orchestration platform without being committed solely to a single lab's class of models.

Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work and automate tasks with any coding agent- Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and more- in one place, each running natively with their own authentication, tools, and configuration options.

Here's a quick 2 minute demo of how I use Proliferate to build Proliferate: ()

I started building Proliferate after onboarding to OpenAI's Codex. Within a few days I was doing virtually all my knowledge work through their desktop app - delegating administrative tasks, communicating specs directly to GPT models, then dispatching them to write code.

And Codex keeps adding features that make it easier and easier to stay in their walled garden, e.g.
1) computer use good enough that I don't really need to visit websites anymore
2) cloud agents for long running tasks
3) pull requests so I don't even need to visit GitHub

All of this makes Codex a magical product that can genuinely be the single horizontal platform you use to do all your knowledge work (see "Codex for everything": https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469).

But as new open source models dropped and I spent weeks inside Codex, I realized I wanted to build my workflows on something that isn't inextricably linked to a single AI lab's models, especially as I automate more recurring work across my team.

Nobody was taking this class of app head-on. Most founders believe you need a vertical to beat the labs - I think the opposite, and that this layer will have a few winners that work across every harness. I believed it enough to pivot my AI QA startup, six figures in revenue, to build one.

That's Proliferate: an open source, self-hostable Codex that preserves your optionality across OpenAI, Anthropic, self-hosted models, and more.

What it does today:
- Works with any coding agent while keeping the native authentication and inference each one offers - your existing subscriptions, Bedrock for Claude Code, your Ollama setup for Codex. Each harness runs natively rather than through a lowest-common-denominator wrapper, and we never middle-man your inference, so you pay whatever you already pay.
- Handles all the provisioning for you: each agent gets an isolated git worktree and a chat you can drop into, so agents work in parallel without stepping on each other or on you.
- Lets your different harnesses communicate and work together through subagents. A parent agent can create another agent in the same workspace - any harness - give it a bounded task, inspect or message it, interrupt it, and receive its result. The child has a durable transcript, and you can promote it into a full session if the thread becomes worth keeping. (I personally love having Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models on review.)
- Runs workflows, the feature I'm most excited about: linear chains of agent and human nodes. You select the harness/model for each agent node, declare inputs, and pass durable documents between nodes. A run can stop at a human gate, be approved, or redo earlier work with a steering prompt. We use them to automate our own cross-agent work, and there are templates for code review, QA, and observability.

The entire project is AGPL-3.0. There is no separate enterprise-only source tree, and Proliferate can't lock you into a model vendor because we don't sell one. The control plane can be installed onto a Docker host with one command, but the self-host path is still beta and I don't want to pretend otherwise. The desktop app is macOS-only today

Next up: self-hostable cloud infrastructure (about a week out), then collaboration primitives so whole teams can work out of the same agent workspace.

This is the first real version of a larger thesis: the next IDE should coordinate a team of agents instead of asking you to commit to one, and it should belong to you. In the limit we want to let you deploy agents that work for you, preserve your optionality, and ideally do a small part in making sure the dissemination of these tools goes well. There is a lot left to build, and I'd especially like hard feedback from people already juggling multiple coding agents or running developer tooling themselves.

The key concept here is agent parallelism through isolated worktrees. Proliferate doesn't just run multiple coding agents; it preserves their native execution environments in separate, git-backed workspaces. Each agent operates in its own branch and working directory, with dedicated tool access and authentication intact. This prevents state collision when agents run concurrently—critical since agents might modify files or dependencies independently.

posts.title: Show HN: Proliferate- an open-source, self-hostable Codex for any coding agent
posts.text:
Hi HN- I'm Pablo, the founder of Proliferate!

Proliferate is an open-source, self-hostable AI IDE that lets you work with any coding agent and automate your work in one place - Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and more - each running natively with their own authentication, tools, and configuration options.

Here's a quick 2 minute demo of how I use Proliferate to build Proliferate: ()

I started building Proliferate after onboarding to OpenAI's Codex. Within a few days I was doing virtually all my knowledge work through their desktop app - delegating administrative tasks, communicating specs directly to GPT models, then dispatching them to write code.

And Codex keeps adding features that make it easier and easier to stay in their walled garden: computer use good enough that I don't really need to visit websites anymore, cloud agents for long running tasks, pull requests so I don't even need to visit GitHub. All of this makes sense - OpenAI wants Codex to be the horizontal platform you do all your knowledge work on (see "Codex for everything": https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47796469).

Codex is a magical product. But as new open source models dropped, I realized I needed to build my workflows on something that isn't inextricably linked to one company's models, especially as I automate more recurring work across my team. And looking at the landscape, I was surprised nobody was directly taking on the Claude and Codex class of app with an ecosystem that embeds every player. I think that's because most founders believe you need to tackle a specific vertical to beat the labs. I think the opposite is true - there will be a few platform winners at this layer that work across every harness - and I believed it enough to pivot my AI QA startup, which was doing six figures in revenue, to go build one.

That's Proliferate: the open source, self-hostable equivalent to Codex, an application and infrastructure layer that preserves your optionality between OpenAI, Anthropic, self-hosted models, and more. What it does today:

- Works with any coding agent while keeping the native authentication and inference each one offers - your existing subscriptions, Bedrock for Claude Code, your Ollama setup for Codex. Each harness runs natively rather than through a lowest-common-denominator wrapper, and we never middle-man your inference, so you pay whatever you already pay.
- Handles all the provisioning for you: each agent gets an isolated git worktree and a chat you can drop into, so agents work in parallel without stepping on each other or on you.
- Lets your different harnesses communicate and work together through subagents. A parent agent can create another agent in the same workspace - any harness - give it a bounded task, inspect or message it, interrupt it, and receive its result. The child has a durable transcript, and you can promote it into a full session if the thread becomes worth keeping. (I personally love having Fable delegate to Codex, with OpenCode models on review.)
- Runs workflows, the feature I'm most excited about: linear chains of agent and human nodes. You select the harness/model for each agent node, declare inputs, and pass durable documents between nodes. A run can stop at a human gate, be approved, or redo earlier work with a steering prompt. We use them to automate our own cross-agent work, and there are templates for code review, QA, and observability.

The entire project is AGPL-3.0. There is no separate enterprise-only source tree, and Proliferate can't lock you into a model vendor because we don't sell one. The control plane can be installed onto a Docker host with one command, but the self-host path is still beta and I don't want to pretend otherwise. The desktop app is macOS-only today. [TODO: insert the ruled localhost-model and Windows/Linux answers.]

This is the first real version of a larger thesis: the next IDE should coordinate a team of agents instead of asking you to commit to one, and it should belong to you. In the limit we want to let you deploy agents that work for you, preserve your optionality, and ideally do a small part in making sure the dissemination of these tools goes well. There is a lot left to build, and I'd especially like hard feedback from people already juggling multiple coding agents or running developer tooling themselves.

comments.content:
The economic model here is a bit unclear. If Proliferate never middle-mans inference and all token spend goes directly to OpenAI, Anthropic, etc., then your revenue has to come from hosting, support, or seats on top of what is essentially an orchestration layer. That is fine as a business, but it means your effective ARPU is constrained by what users already pay for Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, etc. If a small team is paying, say, $400/month to various vendors, it is hard to justify another $400/month just for coordination, especially when each vendor is strongly incentivized to keep "horizontal" features inside its own app. The vendors are not neutral here; their goal is to make Proliferate redundant.

AGPL also cuts both ways. It protects you from being quietly absorbed into someone else’s closed product, but it also deters the most lucrative customers, who are often allergic to copyleft. From a unit economics perspective, the self-host option means a chunk of your most cost-sensitive users will pay you nothing. You are left to monetize enterprises willing to trade higher cash spend for lower integration cost and vendor risk. The hard question strongly for an orchestration layer that the big labs will constantly try to undercut with "free" bundled features?

The comparison to browser evolution is spot on. One key technical nuance worth adding is how Proliferate's native harness approach avoids the pitfall of abstraction leaks that plagued early cross-cloud tools. By maintaining each agent's full execution context rather than forcing compatibility, it sidesteps the uncanny valley where tools work 90% of the time but fail unpredictably on edge cases.

This architecture also enables a hybrid future where proprietary and open models interoperate without either side compromising. That's crucial because unlike browsers, AI agents may retain proprietary advantages in certain domains for years to come.

You're right to catch that detail, but I think the exact count misses the broader pattern at work here. Whether it's three agents or four, the underlying concern is really about platform lock-in and the coordination tax of managing multiple paid services through a middleware layer. The fundamental economics don't shift much between requiring three subscriptions versus four when you're still building on top of services that could be bundled, deprecated, or repriced at any time.

What's more interesting to me is the implicit assumption that running agents in parallel is actually a common workflow need rather than an edge case being elevated to a product thesis. Most developers I know struggle to get value from even one AI coding assistant consistently, let alone orchestrating multiple simultaneously. The technical achievement of unified MCP configuration is elegant, but it optimizes for a use case that may only exist in a narrow band of early adopter scenarios. Before we debate subscription math, I'd want to see evidence that the parallel agent workflow itself solves a real friction point rather than introducing new complexity.

comments.content:
The semantic approach sounds promising, but I see several potential failure modes that could limit its real-world effectiveness. LLMs are notoriously inconsistent with edge cases and might misinterpret domain-specific naming conventions or obfuscated code where attackers deliberately use misleading variable names. The 87% precision rate, while impressive, still means 13% false positives which could overwhelm security teams in large codebases.

A preparedness team is basically a dedicated group whose whole job is to think about tail risks own that mandate end to end, they can run cross cutting evaluations and say, in effect, "we do not ship X until Y risk is understood." comments.content:
The dissolution of OpenAI's preparedness team is not merely a corporate restructuring decision. It represents a fundamental question about our capacity to build institutions that can govern technologies more powerful than themselves. When a company creates systems explicitly designed to assess existential and catastrophic risks, then quietly distributes those responsibilities into product-focused teams, we should recognize this as a test case for whether market incentives can ever align with long-term safety considerations.

The pattern here is troubling because it suggests that safety infrastructure is being treated as overhead rather than as core mission architecture. A preparedness team exists precisely because certain risks cannot be adequately assessed by teams whose primary metrics are deployment speed and capability improvements. By embedding safety evaluation into those same teams, OpenAI has created a structural conflict of interest where the people building and shipping models are simultaneously responsible for determining whether those models should ship at all. This is not how we organize responsibility in other high-stakes domains like nuclear energy or pharmaceuticals.

What ought to happen is straightforward but apparently difficult. Organizations developing frontier AI systems should maintain independent safety evaluation capacity that reports to governance structures insulated from commercial pressure. Ideally this would be mandated externally, but absent regulatory frameworks, we must at minimum demand that companies building potentially transformative technology maintain the institutional capacity to say no to themselves. The fact that OpenAI appears to be dismantling exactly this capacity while approaching an IPO tells us that without external constraints, commercial pressures will systematically erode safety commitments regardless of what any individual actor intends or believes.
